si.short: The international system of units, adopted in 1960: kilogram, metre, second, mole and units built from them, such as the joule (J), watt (W) and newton (N).

vo2max.short: The highest rate at which the body can take up and use oxygen, in L·min⁻¹ (absolute) or mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (per kg of body mass).

joule.short: The SI unit of energy and work: the work done by a force of 1 newton over 1 metre. 1 kJ = 1,000 J; 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.

watt.short: The SI unit of power: one joule per second (W = J·s⁻¹). Power is how fast work is done.

gross-efficiency.short: Mechanical power ÷ metabolic power. In cycling about 20%: the rest of the energy becomes heat.

ftp.short: Functional threshold power: the power a cyclist is meant to hold in a quasi-steady state for about an hour, usually taken as 95% of a 20-minute best. Many riders last well under an hour at it. Used to set zones.

critical-power.short: The power where the power-duration curve levels off: the boundary above which exercise can't reach a steady state and tolerance is limited.

heart-rate-reserve.short: Maximum heart rate minus resting heart rate. A target at x% HRR is: resting HR + x% × HRR (the Karvonen method).

percentage-point.short: The plain difference between two percentages: 20% to 22% is +2 percentage points, which is a 10% relative rise.

half-life.short: For an exponential process, the time for the remaining gap to halve. t½ = 0.69 × τ.

log-scale.short: An axis where equal distances mean equal ratios (×10 or ×2), so seconds and hours fit on one graph.

o2-deficit.short: At the start of exercise, the oxygen that would have been used if VO2 had jumped straight to the demand: the area between demand and actual VO2. Covered mostly by PCr and glycolysis.

confounder.short: A third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome, which makes them look related when one may not cause the other (e.g. talent links training hours and VO2max).
